Earlier this morning you wrote a question and asked it of an entire column of the Toolik
weather table. The answer came back as a **boolean mask**: a `True` or a `False` for every one
of its 11,171 rows.

A mask on its own does not do much for us. The rows it says `True` about are what you are
after, and getting them takes one line of code, which we will write in nearly every session
from here on.

By the end of this session you will be able to:

- write the **filter pattern**, `df[df['col'] > value]`, without looking it up
- filter on text as well as on numbers
- combine two conditions with `&` and `|`, and get the parentheses right
- invert a condition with `~`
- match against a list of values with `.isin()`
- say what `.copy()` is for, and use it when you intend to keep a result

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/openaq_goleta_measurments.csv'
goleta = pd.read_csv(url)
goleta.shape
```

## The pattern

Here it is, whole:

```{python}
goleta[goleta['value'] > 20]
```

Read it from the inside out. `goleta['value'] > 20` is the same kind of mask you wrote this
morning, on a different table: `True` on every row where the value is above 20, `False`
everywhere else. Wrapping it
in `goleta[ ... ]` says "give me the rows where that was `True`."

The line we just ran is the **filter pattern**. The general form is:

```python
df[df['column'] <comparison> value]
```

The `df` appears twice, which looks redundant until you see what each one is doing. The inner
one builds the question, the outer one applies the answer, and they are the same table both
times.

Give the result a name if you want to use it later:

```{python}
high_readings = goleta[goleta['value'] > 20]
high_readings.shape
```

115 rows out of 1,962. Compare the shapes before and after, and you can see exactly how many
rows the filter kept:

```{python}
print('before:', goleta.shape)
print('after: ', high_readings.shape)
```

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 Filtering never changes the original. `goleta` still has all 1,962 rows. You get back a
new, smaller table, and if you don't give it a name it is displayed once and then discarded.
`.rename()` followed the same rule yesterday.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Filter `goleta` to the rows where `value` is **below zero**. How many are there? A
concentration below zero is not physically possible, so make a note of what you find; we will
deal with values like these on Day 4.
:::

## Filtering on text

The same pattern works on text columns. Use `==` for an exact match:

```{python}
ozone = goleta[goleta['parameter'] == 'o3']
ozone.head()
```

```{python}
ozone.shape
```

711 ozone readings. Text comparisons are exact and case-sensitive, so `'O3'` would have
matched nothing at all:

```{python}
goleta[goleta['parameter'] == 'O3'].shape
```

An empty result is not an error. Zero rows is a real answer, and it usually means a spelling or
capitalization problem rather than a fact about the data.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Filter `goleta` to the `pm25` readings and store them in a variable called `pm25`. How many
rows? Check your number against `goleta['parameter'].value_counts()` from yesterday.
:::

## Why filtering matters for the Goleta data

Yesterday you found that `goleta['value']` stacks three different pollutants, in two different
units, in one column. Mixing three pollutants together made `.describe()` on the whole column
meaningless.

Filtering is the fix:

```{python}
goleta['value'].describe()
```

```{python}
goleta[goleta['parameter'] == 'pm25']['value'].describe()
```

The first summary averages micrograms per cubic metre together with parts per million, which
gives a mean that describes no substance at all. The second one describes 734 particulate
readings, all in µg/m³, and only the second one tells you anything about the air in Goleta.

## Two conditions at once

`&` means "and". Every comparison gets its own parentheses:

```{python}
goleta[(goleta['parameter'] == 'pm25') & (goleta['value'] > 9)]
```

128 hours where fine particulate matter was above 9 µg/m³, which is the annual air quality
standard the US EPA set in 2024, tightened from the 12 µg/m³ that had stood since 2012.

`|` means "or":

```{python}
particulates = goleta[(goleta['parameter'] == 'pm25') | (goleta['parameter'] == 'pm10')]
particulates.shape
```

Each side of an `&` or a `|` can itself be a two-part condition. When it is, wrap that whole
side in a further pair of parentheses so the two questions stay separate:

```{python}
either_pollutant_high = goleta[
    ((goleta['parameter'] == 'pm25') & (goleta['value'] > 9))
    | ((goleta['parameter'] == 'pm10') & (goleta['value'] > 20))
]
either_pollutant_high.shape
```

240 rows: 128 hours of pm25 above 9, plus 112 hours of pm10 above 20. Read the line from the
inside out. Each innermost pair is one comparison, each middle pair is one complete question
about one pollutant, and the `|` joins the two questions.

:::{.callout-important title="The parentheses are not optional"}
Leave them out and you get an error that has nothing to do with what you meant:

```python
goleta[goleta['parameter'] == 'pm25' & goleta['value'] > 9]
```

`&` binds more tightly than `==` and `>`, so Python combines the wrong pieces before it ever
gets to your comparison.

The rule that avoids all of this: **put parentheses around each comparison you join with `&` or
`|`.** A comparison is something with `==`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` or `!=` in it. A method call
like `.isin([...])` is not a comparison and does not need its own pair, though adding them does
no harm if you would rather not think about which is which.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Find the ozone readings above 0.04 ppm. Then, using the two-level shape above, find the readings
that are **either** ozone above 0.04 ppm **or** pm25 above 20 µg/m³. How many rows does each
give you?
:::

## Turning a condition around with `~`

`~` inverts a mask: every `True` becomes `False` and every `False` becomes `True`.

```{python}
not_ozone = goleta[~(goleta['parameter'] == 'o3')]
not_ozone.shape
```

1,251 rows, which is 1,962 minus the 711 ozone readings. You could have written
`!=` here and gotten the same answer:

```{python}
goleta[goleta['parameter'] != 'o3'].shape
```

`~` is most useful when the condition is more complicated than a single comparison, and you
would rather say "not that" than rewrite the whole condition backwards.

## Matching a list of values with `.isin()`

Writing `(col == 'a') | (col == 'b') | (col == 'c')` gets tedious fast. `.isin()` takes a
**list** and matches any of its members:

```{python}
particulates = goleta[goleta['parameter'].isin(['pm25', 'pm10'])]
particulates.shape
```

Same 1,251 rows as the `|` version above, in a line that stays readable when the list grows.

The argument is an ordinary Python list, so you can build it first and pass it by name:

```{python}
of_interest = ['pm25', 'pm10']
goleta[goleta['parameter'].isin(of_interest)].shape
```

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 Call `.isin()` on the **column**, not on the DataFrame: `df['col'].isin([...])`. It returns
a mask, exactly like a comparison does, so it goes in the same place inside the brackets.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Build a list called `keep_parameters` holding `'o3'` and `'pm10'`, then use `.isin()` to
filter `goleta` down to those two pollutants. Check your row count against the two numbers in
`goleta['parameter'].value_counts()`; they should add up.
:::

## Keeping a result with `.copy()`

Once you have a subset you like, you will usually want to keep working on it, and often that
means adding a column to it later this week.

When you plan to keep and modify a filtered result, say `.copy()`:

```{python}
pm25 = goleta[goleta['parameter'] == 'pm25'].copy()
pm25.shape
```

`.copy()` gives you a table of your own, with no remaining connection to `goleta`. Without it,
the subset you get back may still be tied to the original table. When you then try to change
the subset, you get either a warning that is hard to interpret or a change that silently never
happens.

The habit is easy to state:

> If the filtered result is going to be a **thing you keep and change**, end the line with
> `.copy()`. If you are just looking at it, don't bother.

```{python}
pm25.head()
```

:::{.callout-caution title="A warning you will meet"}
`SettingWithCopyWarning` shows up when a change you have written could apply either to the
subset or to the original table, and the code as written does not say which one you meant. It
is not always a real problem, but it is always worth reading! Adding `.copy()` at the point
where you made the subset is usually the fix.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Make a `.copy()` of the ozone readings called `ozone`, then confirm with `.shape` and
`.head()` that you have what you expect. Keep it in your notebook; you'll use it in the next
session.
:::

## Putting it together

A real filter is usually two or three of these ideas in one line:

```{python}
summer_particulates = goleta[
    goleta['parameter'].isin(['pm25', 'pm10']) & (goleta['value'] > 15)
].copy()

summer_particulates.shape
```

```{python}
summer_particulates[['parameter', 'value', 'unit', 'datetimeLocal']].head()
```

Notice that the filter is broken across several lines inside the square brackets. Python allows
a line break anywhere inside a pair of brackets, and a long filter is much easier to read that
way.

## Key points

- The **filter pattern** is `df[df['col'] <comparison> value]`. The inner `df` builds the
  mask; the outer one applies it.
- Filtering returns a **new** DataFrame. Assign it to a name to keep it.
- `==` matches text exactly, and is case-sensitive. An empty result is an answer, not an error.
- Combine conditions with `&` for and, `|` for or, `~` for not. **Every comparison needs its
  own parentheses.**
- `df['col'].isin([...])` matches any value in a list, and replaces a pile of `|`.
- End a filter with `.copy()` when you plan to keep the result and change it later.
